findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The double-checked locking pattern is incomplete: after acquiring the write lock there is no second nil-check of entryPointAssetsCache, so every concurrent first-request goroutine proceeds to rebuild the asset list and overwrite the cache. Under a cold-start burst (many concurrent requests before first cache fill), each goroutine performs the full filesystem scan/setup of GetWebAssets redundantly instead of one; whoever gets bitten: operators seeing repeated slow first responses and redundant work in non-Dev environments, and the cache write from the slowest goroutine silently replaces a potentially newer one.

[BUG] The cache check is not re-evaluated after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent first requests each rebuild and overwrite the assets. Under concurrent cold-start requests in non-Dev, N simultaneous goroutines all see nil, all take the write lock in turn, and each re-runs the expensive build (dist scan / checksum work) instead of the intended single build; the last writer wins the cache, so callers receive different EntryPointAssets instances for the same key, defeating the cache exactly when load is highest.

[ADVISORY] The new locking behavior is introduced with no test coverage anywhere in the diff. A regression in the read-cache fast path (e.g., returning the cache even in Dev, or a missed Unlock on an error return in the elided build section) ships undetected; the diff contains no test-shaped files or assertions exercising the new entryPointAssetsCacheMu paths, so the concurrency contract of GetWebAssets is unverified.

[BUG] The double-checked locking pattern is broken: after acquiring the write lock the code never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache, so every concurrent cold-start request re-runs the full asset scan under mutual exclusion instead of one request doing the work and the rest reusing the result. During concurrent startup/first requests in non-Dev, N simultaneous callers serialize on entryPointAssetsCacheMu and each performs the expensive directory walk; the added lock converts a previously parallel redundant read into serialized redundant work and holds the write lock for the entire scan duration, blocking all Dev-env readers on every request (Dev never caches, so every Dev request takes the write lock).

[ADVISORY] The PR adds concurrency control (sync.RWMutex) and a new TODO comment, which is a race-condition fix plus code hygiene, not the stated 'asset optimization' work — it is implementation not traceable to the PR's stated intent. Reviewers and future archaeologists tracing this diff cannot tell why the lock was introduced here (no data race issue is referenced); if a separate race-fix PR lands, the two changes will conflict and the duplicated effort surfaces as merge friction for whoever reconciles them.

[ADVISORY] GetWebAssets holds the exclusive write lock across the entire asset-building operation, blocking all concurrent readers for the duration of the filesystem scan. Under a burst of cold-start requests (or any Dev-mode traffic, where the cache-return path is skipped), every request serializes on the mutex while one goroutine walks the disk; the first slow/hung disk read stalls all web asset responses for all users, a degraded-availability cliff introduced by moving from a race-y-but-parallel read to a globally serialized critical section.

[ADVISORY] The double-checked locking pattern never re-checks the cache after acquiring the write lock, so every request that arrived during the first build rebuilds the assets from scratch and overwrites the cache. N concurrent cold-start requests issue N sequential (lock-serialized) full filesystem scans instead of one — the lock added to fix a data race turns the cold path from N parallel scans into N serialized scans with the same redundancy, where a one-line `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return ... }` recheck after Lock() would collapse them to one.

[ADVISORY] The cache is keyed by nothing and validated against only cfg.Env, so a GetWebAssets call with a different cfg (e.g. a different static-asset root, custom appSubUrl, or enterprise plugin path) silently returns the first caller's assets to all later callers. Any deployment or test harness constructing multiple setting.Cfg values in one process (common in Grafana integration tests and multi-tenant setups) gets cross-contaminated web assets; the TODO comment acknowledges the global-state problem but the new mutex entrenches it by making the global the coordination point rather than moving ownership to cfg.

[ADVISORY] The double-checked locking is incomplete: after acquiring the write lock, GetWebAssets never re-reads entryPointAssetsCache, so N concurrent requests on a cold cache in a non-Dev environment all serialize and each fully recomputes the asset scan, with only the last write surviving. Operators of production instances after a restart see N redundant filesystem scans and lock contention on the first burst of asset requests instead of one; behavior is functionally correct but the caching objective the original code encoded is silently weakened under concurrency introduced by this very change.

[ADVISORY] In Dev mode the code unconditionally acquires the exclusive write lock (entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()) on every request, serializing all concurrent asset requests behind a global mutex while each performs the (uncached, never-populated-in-Dev) filesystem scan. A developer running Grafana in Dev with concurrent page loads / multiple browser tabs hits a global lock convoy: each request waits for the previous request's full filesystem walk, turning a previously parallel path into fully serialized I/O; latency scales linearly with concurrent dev-mode requests.

[ADVISORY] The double-checked locking pattern is incomplete: after acquiring the write lock the code never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache, so every concurrent cold-start request performs the full asset-building work sequentially rather than only the first. On a cold start under load (non-Dev), N simultaneous requests each enqueue on the write lock and each re-runs the entire directory scan/asset enumeration when one run would suffice — wasted work and extended lock hold time; correct behavior, wasted cost.

goldens.comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

adjudication.rationale: After the initial RLock/RUnlock, the code conditionally returns based on `ret`, but once it falls through it unconditionally takes the write lock (`entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`) without re-checking whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` while this goroutine was waiting. From the diff shown, this enables the classic double-checked-locking mistake: concurrent cold-start calls can each observe `nil`, then serialize on the write lock and still each proceed to rebuild instead of the second/third callers returning the cached value once available.

adjudication.rationale: The diff implements a read-then-write lock around a global cache: it RLocks to read `entryPointAssetsCache`, returns early only when `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil`, otherwise it takes `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and (per diff) proceeds to compute assets while holding the write lock. There is no re-check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent cold-start callers that all observed `nil` will serialize and each will redo the expensive work under the write lock rather than one doing the work and the rest reusing the populated cache. This is a performance/locking contention issue grounded in the shown code, not a functional correctness bug.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global RWMutex and takes an exclusive `Lock()` with `defer Unlock()` before the asset-building work (the function continues after the shown hunk). That means any call that misses the early-return path (including all `cfg.Env == setting.Dev` calls, where the cache path is skipped) will hold the write lock for the duration of the filesystem/asset build, blocking all concurrent readers and other writers. This is a concrete concurrency/performance/availability regression risk introduced by the change, but it’s not a functional correctness defect per se.

adjudication.rationale: In GetWebAssets, the function reads the cached pointer under RLock, returns if non-nil, then unconditionally takes the write Lock and proceeds to build assets without re-checking entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. From the diff, this means concurrent cold-start callers that saw nil before the first build completes will serialize behind the Lock and each still perform the expensive build even if a prior waiter already populated the cache. This is a concrete, diff-grounded inefficiency caused by the missing second cache check; it’s not clearly a functional correctness bug based on what’s shown.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `entryPointAssetsCache` is a single global `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` returned for any non-dev call (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil { return ret, nil }`) without considering any other `cfg` fields. Adding the mutex makes this global cache thread-safe but does not address (and arguably further cements) the design where all callers share one cache entry regardless of which `cfg` was passed. Whether this is a concrete runtime bug depends on how `cfg` is used later in `GetWebAssets` (not shown in the diff), but the review concern about global, unkeyed caching is directly supported by the code shown.

From what’s shown, any goroutine that misses the initial read check will proceed into the locked section and recompute work even if another goroutine populated the cache just before it acquired the write lock, causing serialized redundant computation on a cold cache. This is a concurrency/performance/caching-objective issue rather than a functional correctness defect.
